name: Femi Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does your working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and lead a small carpentry crew on building sites. I set out openings, check the first frame and still carry timber when we are short of hands. My trade certificate taught the basics; years of uneven walls taught the rest. The pay is poor for a lead, and the mortgage and two schoolchildren leave us with less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I would say that a faster order sheet is welcome if the timber still arrives in the right size. An AI list cannot plane a door that catches on a building site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel relief about the trade, but the mortgage is already tight on my wages. My partner and I have less than one month of bills put aside, and there are few other construction crews nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the frame crew and checking deliveries against the drawing. I would put a small part of each paid week into a separate emergency pot if our bills allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy rather than frightened by the AI. The wage problem was here before the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which ordinary bill makes that thin cushion matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage payment lands just after my pay, and school lunches and travel take the rest. One cancelled week of site work would make us choose what to delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let the software order timber without you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I use AI now and then to compare a list, but I sign off the measurement on the building site myself.

say: I would **welcome** quicker ordering if the delivered timber still matches the openings I measured.
I would **keep** checking the first door and the delivery before the crew cuts anything.
think: My **carpentry** work looks steady in this picture, but one lost paid week would strain the mortgage.
I **use** AI occasionally for a list, yet a screen cannot see an uneven wall.
do: **Keep** leading the framing crew and measure delivered timber against each building opening.
**Save** a little from paid weeks after mortgage and school costs if money remains.
feel: **Uneasy** about thin savings even if construction work continues.
S0.quote: An AI list cannot plane a door that catches on a building site.
fieldNote: His **confidence** in skilled carpentry is tempered by lower pay and less than one month of savings.
**Occasional** AI use helps with lists, while measured timber and paid site weeks determine his household security.

steps.text: Keep leading carpentry crew and checking timber deliveries
Save part of paid site wages when mortgage and school bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that the office may order and schedule faster, but the door still has to fit. If the firm trims office time, I would ask whether site targets and our paid hours change too. A shorter AI schedule could leave my carpentry crew with a shorter paid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I fear the same manager might use shorter planning time as a reason to squeeze our price per job. My partner has steady work, but our two incomes leave almost no buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the carpentry shifts and ask for the revised schedule and wage terms in writing. I would try the AI ordering tool only after a colleague demonstrates it on a real job, then save any extra paid hours rather than count on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about a possible cut in paid hours, though I can still check the terms and adjust. I would not call the computer the problem if the firm chooses the rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you try the ordering tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see a colleague enter actual room sizes and compare the delivery with our tape measurements. I will use it if it survives that check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the firm cuts your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for more paid framing days first. If the cut holds, I would ask the few other local crews about a posted lead role at a wage that covers our mortgage.

say: I would **ask** whether faster office schedules change the crew’s paid hours or rates.
I would **test** the new ordering tool against a real wall measurement before using it.
think: A **cut** in site hours would reach my mortgage faster than any change in paperwork.
I can **learn** a proven tool, but management still sets the wage.
do: **Ask** the site manager for written paid-hour and wage terms when schedules change.
**Try** AI ordering after a colleague demonstrates it with measured building openings.
**Save** wages from any extra paid framing hours after essential bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible hours cut, with some room to question the terms.
S1.quote: A shorter AI schedule could leave my carpentry crew with a shorter paid week.
fieldNote: He **accepts** change after proof on site and separates software speed from a management pay decision.
**Thin** savings mean even an indirect hours reduction is a realistic household risk, despite his composed speech.

steps.text: Keep carpentry shifts while checking written paid-hour terms
Test proven AI ordering against actual building measurements
Save pay from extra framing hours after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I would say thinking AI can price a job in 2028, when I am forty-five, but it cannot frame a wall by hand then. The 2031 robots worry me more because I will be forty-eight with a mortgage still running. A framing robot in 2031 could eat my paid week before my mortgage gets any smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big loss of site hours if robots take routine framing around 2031. I lie awake working out which bill would go first; less than a month saved is almost no runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the manager which paid carpentry work is expected through 2031 and seek written terms. In the first year after robots actually arrive, I would keep available shifts, cut nonessential spending and apply only for a posted nearby site-lead job whose wage covers the mortgage; there are few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed when I picture a robot doing the square frames we build every week. I know I can still set out awkward rooms, but I cannot assume enough of those jobs remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes first from the household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would pause weekend outings and nonessential house work before touching the children’s school travel. If paid hours fell deeply, we would have to discuss a mortgage payment plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look for another lead job if local vacancies are rare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know the trade and cannot move our children on a guess. I would apply only to an actual nearby vacancy with a clear wage, not resign to chase a rumour.

say: **Thinking** AI would affect building estimates first; hand framing faces robots around 2031.
I would **ask** for honest paid-hour plans rather than pretend the crews are secure.
think: I **expect** major paid-hour loss from routine framing, and the mortgage calculation keeps me awake.
The **few** local jobs mean a vacancy and bill-covering pay must precede any move.
do: **Ask** the builder for written framing hours expected through the 2031 robot arrival.
**Cut** outings if paid carpentry hours actually fall.
**Apply** for posted nearby lead role only if wage covers mortgage and school costs.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major income loss and nights spent calculating bills.
S2.quote: A framing robot in 2031 could eat my paid week before my mortgage gets any smaller.
fieldNote: His **alarm** follows an expected major loss of routine framing hours and explicit sleeplessness about bills.
He **keeps** the 2028 thinking change separate from hands-on robots around 2031 and requires a real local offer.

steps.text: Keep available site shifts while asking for written future hours
Cut household outings after a paid-hour loss
Apply for posted nearby lead job with bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that 2031 thinking AI changes plans and ordering when I am forty-eight, while 2034 robots reach framing when I am fifty-one. Three extra years give me time to prove I can check tricky building work. I cannot spend a week of carpentry wages on a course for a job nobody has posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect routine hours to shrink, but I could prepare without leaving a paid job. A course fee or unpaid training week would use the little money our mortgage has left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the employer for paid time and full funding for an on-site inspection course, and enroll only if they provide both. In the first year after 2031 I would keep leading frames and, if I complete that course, apply only to posted local inspection jobs that pay enough for mortgage and school bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious, but the longer lead time lets me make a testable plan. The first written vacancy matters more than a promise about a future trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course teach that you do not already do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would teach formal sign-off on frame alignment and robot-built sections, not basic carpentry. I already know how to spot a bowed stud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer offers funding but no paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on framing shifts and decline for now. We cannot lose a week of wages to buy a chance at a job that may not exist.

say: The 2031 **change** reaches building plans before robots reach framing around 2034.
I would **use** the lead time to qualify for physical inspection if paid training exists.
think: A **funded** course still fails our budget if it requires unpaid weeks.
I **need** a posted local inspection vacancy with wages that cover the household before changing jobs.
do: **Enroll** in funded inspection course only with paid training time.
**Keep** leading framing shifts while completing any paid inspection training.
**Apply** for posted local inspection job only at mortgage-covering wage.
feel: **Anxious** about routine hours, but clearer time allows a conditional route.
S3.quote: I cannot spend a week of carpentry wages on a course for a job nobody has posted.
fieldNote: His **training** decision depends jointly on full course funding and paid time, not curiosity alone.
A **real** local vacancy and household-covering wage remain essential to any switch from framing.

steps.text: Enroll in funded inspection course with paid time
Keep paid framing shifts while training
Apply for posted local inspector role with bill-covering wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that I will be fifty-three when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and fifty-six when capable building robots arrive around 2039. I would use the warning to build a checking route while still earning on site. A decade before building robots is useful only if my carpentry wage reaches every mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become the person who checks repair work and teaches new carpenters to measure before accepting a machine result. Yet a plan that needs unpaid study is useless with our thin savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the lead carpentry shifts and put a small new amount from each paid week toward a larger cushion after bills. If a funded, paid-time assessor course becomes available, I would take it; after completing it I would apply only to posted nearby assessor jobs paying enough for our household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant robot date and anxious about money right now. The extra years are useful only if the wage keeps arriving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the savings plan is working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark each actual transfer from wages on our kitchen calendar. If no money remains after the mortgage, I would write zero rather than claim we saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave carpentry as soon as you had a certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would wait for a posted assessor vacancy nearby and check the wage against mortgage and school costs before leaving paid site work.

say: A **decade** gives me time to build savings and consider physical quality checks.
I would **teach** measuring on site, where an apprentice can see a crooked frame.
think: My **current** low pay makes the next mortgage instalment more urgent than a 2039 machine.
**Training** and a later job still need paid time, full funding and a real local wage.
do: **Save** a new amount from paid carpentry wages after mortgage and school bills.
**Complete** funded assessor course only if training time is paid.
**Apply** for posted nearby assessor job only at household-covering wage.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant robots and anxious about today’s thin cash margin.
S4.quote: A decade before building robots is useful only if my carpentry wage reaches every mortgage payment.
fieldNote: His **ten-year** plan includes new transfers from wages rather than treating existing cash as new saving.
He **remains** attached to skilled site work and requires funded paid training plus a real local vacancy.

steps.text: Save new amounts from paid carpentry wages after bills
Complete assessor course only with funding and paid time
Apply for posted local assessor role with bill-covering pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one worries me most, because I expect framing hours to fall by 2031 and the mortgage keeps me awake. What helps is a written hours plan, paid training that costs us nothing, and an actual local job at a wage that covers the house and school costs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the family has between paydays. A skilled carpenter with less than a month saved cannot wait for a new trade to become fashionable. My trade certificate can prove I know a frame; it cannot cover a missing week of wages.

headlineQuote: My trade certificate can prove I know a frame; it cannot cover a missing week of wages.
portrait: **Femi** is a forty-three-year-old lead carpenter with a trade certificate, a partner, two schoolchildren and a mortgage.
His **pay** is low for his job, savings cover less than one month, and few similar roles exist nearby.
He **uses** AI occasionally once a tool is proven against real building measurements.
**Fast** robots make him expect major framing-hour loss; more lead time permits conditional paid inspection training.
biggestWorry: The 2028/2031 **fast** scenario brings expected major paid-hour loss from framing robots while his mortgage remains due.
whatWouldHelp: **Written** paid-hour plans, fully funded training on paid time and a posted local job with household-covering wages would help.
